definitions.gloss: offertory box; donation box at a shrine or temple
definitions.explanation: Found at the front of Japanese shrines and temples for monetary offerings.

examples.japanese: {賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}にお{金|かね}を{入|い}れた。
examples.english: I put money into the offertory box.

examples.japanese: {神社|じんじゃ}の{賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}に{五円|ごえん}{玉|だま}を{投|な}げ{入|い}れた。
examples.english: I tossed a five-yen coin into the shrine's offertory box.

examples.japanese: {正月|しょうがつ}には{賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}の{前|まえ}に{長|なが}い{行列|ぎょうれつ}ができる。
examples.english: During New Year's, long lines form in front of the offertory box.

notes:
Composed of {賽銭|さいせん} (monetary offering) + {箱|ばこ} (box). The large wooden box placed in front of the main hall at Japanese shrines and temples where visitors toss coins as part of their prayer or wish.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}にお{金|かね}を{入|い}れる: to put money in the offertory box
- {賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}の{前|まえ}で{手|て}を{合|あ}わせる: to put hands together in front of the offertory box
- {賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}{泥棒|どろぼう}: offertory box thief

CULTURAL NOTE:
The standard worship procedure at a Shinto shrine is to toss a coin into the {賽銭|さいせん}{箱|ばこ}, ring the bell, bow twice, clap twice, pray, and bow once more. Five-yen coins ({五円|ごえん}{玉|だま}) are popular because {五円|ごえん} sounds like {御縁|ごえん} (divine connection). At Buddhist temples, the procedure differs slightly, with no clapping.

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {賽銭|さいせん}: the offering itself (the money)
- {奉納|ほうのう}{箱|ばこ}: votive offering box (for non-monetary offerings)
- {募金|ぼきん}{箱|ばこ}: donation box, collection box (secular)
